lignes.texte: “A little weed now and again never killed anyone.” At least, that’s what Alex thinks as he lights
up every day. What started as a way to relax after a long workday has spiralled
into a decade long habit. But Alex thinks he’s fine.
He considers himself as the ultimate “high-functioning stoner”.
What he didn’t realize is that his brain is panicking. To survive the daily chemical flood,
it has deployed a defense mechanism that has fundamentally altered his biology.
What happens in the human body after you flood it with THC for 3,650 days straight?
This is the year-by-year biological autopsy of a 10 year habit,
and how a “natural” plant rewires a human life.
22 year old Alex has just stepped into the corporate world. He’s a high achiever,
landing an intense, high pressure position straight out of college. But the long hours and
relentless workload start to stress him out pretty quickly. He used to smoke weed once in a while,
but now he starts smoking daily to take the edge off. It relaxes him, stops his mind
from racing and helps him sleep. It’s win win… or so he thinks.
But beneath the surface, the neuro-hijack has begun.
To protect itself from constant overstimulation, his brain starts retreating. His reward system
is slowly downregulated, something his brain deems necessary to survive the tsunami of THC
bombarding it every day. Like a city turning off sections of its power grid to prevent a
massive surge, Alex’s brain is altering its own baseline just to keep the lights on.
How much of that grid is about to go dark… forever?
It’s year one of his habit. Alex is going through life working hard, seeing his friends,
and even getting an excellent performance review. He’s truly a “high functioning stoner”.
But things are starting to change in his life in ways he’s not even realizing.
Throughout college, he loved playing his guitar in the evenings, but he hasn’t touched it in months.
He’s just not in the mood. The creative drive is gone. He also used to hit the gym 3 to 4 times
a week, but after starting his daily habit, his motivation tanked. The workouts dropped to twice
a week, then once, then stopped all together. Alex thinks it’s because of the long hours he’s
working and lack of energy. And he’s getting irritable.
Even when he gets a full night’s sleep, he wakes up feeling a little cranky and tired.
He’s having fewer dreams, but he doesn’t know why that is… not yet.
By the end of the first year, Alex is smoking more weed than he ever did. His system has
built up a tolerance. Now needs larger amounts of THC just to get to a baseline relaxed state.
Doctors administering medical marijuana recently found out just how fast that tolerance builds up.
One study found that patients experienced 0.5% less relief with each session of
medical marijuana. It might sound tiny, but after 20 sessions it adds up to a
10% reduction in symptom relief. For someone using weed daily,
that means their tolerance to weed builds up in a matter of weeks. Not years.
While Alex isn’t using marijuana medically, he is using it to soothe his symptoms of anxiety
and stress. But now, it's just not doing the job like it used to. So he smokes more frequently.
In his second and third years of daily use, Alex is socializing outside his house less and less.
Because Alex has unknowingly become one of the 30% of daily users who develop Cannabis Use Disorder,
or CUD. Because he’s a chronic daily smoker, he’s at especially high risk for the disorder.
CUD means someone who compulsively continues to use marijuana despite
it having adverse effects on their daily life, mental health and physical wellbeing.
The few times Alex has been out with friends all evening and skipped smoking weed,
he’s visibly restless. He’s just fixated on getting back to his place and lighting up.
So as the year goes on, he decides he’s going to find a way to smoke weed while
out and about. Even though he’s getting into his car later; he’ll take the risk of driving high.
Eventually, at the start of his third year of daily use,
Alex is seeing his friends way less than he used to.
He’s starting to drift away from anyone who doesn’t want to just hang out and smoke weed.
By the end of the year, Alex is wondering if he has ADHD. His working memory is cratering.
He’s missing critical deadlines at work because the due date vanished from his mind.
He’s failing to complete tasks he said he’d personally take care of. His short term memory
is wiping the second he takes them on. But the truth is, he doesn’t really care.
Alex is bored at work and doesn’t feel like doing anything work related some days.
What he thinks is corporate burnout is actually something called “amotivational syndrome”.
Sustained daily cannabis use results in a devastating drop in everyday drive.
When THC enters Alex’s system, it causes a surge of dopamine. It hijacks his brain
and gives him the feeling of contentment. By using weed daily, Alex is rewarding his
brain repeatedly without expending an ounce of real world effort. He’s hardwiring his brain
to abandon any non-weed sources of fulfillment. To confirm this, scientists ran a 4 year study on
college students. They forced subjects to perform a series of simple tasks for financial reward.
Meanwhile, researchers were imaging their brains in real time to see the fallout.
Students who were using weed the most had decreased activity in their reward center when
anticipating their money at the end of the task set. Scientists concluded, “as cannabis alters
the brain’s reward center, regular users begin to anticipate less reward from non-cannabis sources.”
That’s why Alex’s desire to put in effort for any other tasks that can
cause a dopamine surge – like achieving a personal goal - has gone out the window.
Over time, weed blunts the brain’s dopamine production. Even if Alex got back into his
hobbies or social life, he would receive less dopamine as a reward. It’s part of the
reason Alex isn’t that interested in leaving his house or why he just doesn’t care about his job.
But instead of quitting, Alex ups his weed intake. He’s convinced that all the stress from his
career is making his anxiety worse. Weed is his only escape.
At least, that’s what he thinks. In fact, daily cannabis use can take a toll on
mental health, leading to symptoms like worsening anxiety, depression, or general emotional
distress. Many people start using weed daily to self-medicate and deal with these issues. But over
time, frequent THC use will only exacerbate them. Why? Because the long-term effects of chronic
marijuana use are actually the opposite of its short-term results.
That’s most obvious when it comes to sleep. Plenty of people use weed before bed to help
unwind and sleep more easily. In the short term, low doses of marijuana work like a sedative.
People fall asleep faster and stay asleep longer. But after long term and increasing use,
the effects on sleep are reversed. Just like with prolonged alcohol use.
Because while Alex is taking weed to help him relax and sleep, he doesn’t know that THC binds
to brain receptors that specifically suppress the REM stage. That’s when the brain clears out a lot
of its cellular waste to reset for the next day. And Alex’s brain?
It’s not doing that as much as it should. It’s like running a computer for years without
ever clearing the cache or updating the OS. Things are going to get backed up and slower.
REM sleep not only helps the brain process stressful events, sharpen working memory,
and strengthen brain cell connections; it also lowers stress hormones and supports
mental health in general. The less REM sleep Alex gets, the more he feels some low-level stress in
his system… even when he doesn’t know why. Which is why his anxiety is flaring up.
Alex traded in better overall mental health and stress levels for temporary stress relief.
And he didn’t even know it. Things get worse in his fourth and fifth year
of daily use. At this point, Alex can’t skip a day of weed use without feeling cravings. Evening
weed use has moved up to early afternoon use and on the weekends, occasional morning use as well.
His work performance is rapidly declining. His boss has stopped giving him some of the bigger
responsibilities he used to. Partly because Alex doesn’t seem as interested in a promotion anyway.
And partly because it’s increasingly hard for Alex to deal with complex decision-making.
Because at this point Alex is actively losing grey matter.
THC, the main active ingredient in cannabis, attaches to cannabinoid type 1 – CB1 – receptors
in the brain. When these receptors are overwhelmed, the brain begins a survival shutdown.
It down-regulates the number and availability of active CB1 receptors by up to 20%.
CB1 receptors are scattered all throughout the brain; though they congregate in heavy
concentrations in critical regions. These include the medial temporal cortex, temporal pole,
insula, and orbitofrontal cortex. For the non-neuroscientists among us, these are
the areas that deal with motivational, emotional, and affective processing.
The reduction in receptors triggers a reduction of grey matter in these regions.
While research is still too limited to show how much grey matter decreases,
we know the hippocampus and orbitofrontal cortex are the most affected.
The hippocampus is responsible for important human survival traits like decision making,
processing rewards and reading social norms. It also controls how someone responds to adversity.
That probably explains why Alex can’t handle complex tasks at work anymore.
As these brain regions shrink, Alex’s ability to weigh options and decide begins to suffer.
He can’t predict the potential results of decisions like he used to.
His lack of motivation might also be correlated with his hippocampus decreasing in volume.
What does this result in? A radical shift in his behavior. And Alex’s belief that he’s a
“high functioning stoner” is about to shatter. Even if his colleagues can’t tell he’s high,
daily weed use is still influencing every single aspect of his life.
And it’s starting to make long-term changes in his brain structure and performance.
Scientists in New Zealand studied more than 1,000 participants over 38 years, dividing them into
never-smokers, and then by frequency of weed use. Their research shows that people who were long
term smokers experienced a drop of 5-6 IQ points. Not that they were 5 IQ points lower than their
non-smoker peers. They actually lost IQ over years of habitual weed use.
While this decrease in IQ was evident across the board, another study found that the
“greatest impairments were for the domains of executive functioning and processing speed.”
The former being the “management center” of the brain. The part that motivates you to plan, set,
and execute goals; the latter is the amount of time your brain needs to take in information,
make sense of it, and act accordingly. Since Alex’s management center is a
little blunted, together with his “amotivational syndrome”,
it’s creating a vicious cycle. He’s getting less and less done… but needs more time to do it all.
Which is why the term “high functioning stoner” is a lie.
Alex doesn’t realize this yet. The effects have accumulated slowly over time and he has bought
into the myth that weed has zero harmful effects. Marijuana was overly demonized and lied about for
a very long time. Everyone from schoolteachers and parents to local DARE officers would warn about
ridiculous - and unrealistic sounding - “dangers” of weed to scare students into never trying it.
However, when marijuana was decriminalized or even legalized in some states,
it became clear these scare tactics weren’t true. The pendulum then swung to the other side,
and people started believing marijuana wasn’t bad for you at all. In 2002, around 50% of
people thought smoking marijuana was harmful. In 2014, that number had dropped to 33%. Even as
it became 4 times more potent, and people became more aware about the dangers of substance abuse,
marijuana mostly gets a free pass. But by the sixth and seventh years of weed use,
it’s not just Alex’s brain experiencing changes. He is starting to notice physical symptoms.
Coughing while smoking weed is entirely normal and expected. But Alex has developed
a chronic cough, whether he’s smoking or not. There’s a persistent myth that smoking weed is
not harmful to users, unlike tobacco. But smoke is smoke. Inhaling it frequently, no matter what’s in
it, will damage a person’s respiratory system. The American Lung Association found that
“...although not as carcinogenic… marijuana smoke contains toxins and
carcinogens similar to those in tobacco smoke.” In heavy smokers, weed use has caused air pockets
in between the lungs, as well as in the lungs themselves. The smoke kills the lung’s defensive
cells, the ones that remove dust and germs, making them more vulnerable to infection.
This leads to symptoms like chronic cough, phlegm production, wheeze, and acute bronchitis.
CT scans have shown that people who only smoke marijuana had “greater airway thickening and
inflammation as well as emphysema compared to both nonsmokers and tobacco-only smokers”.
It’s a turning point in Alex’s future. One study found that marijuana smokers face
significantly higher risks of developing conditions like bullous lung disease.
This is where air gets trapped in the lungs and damages them, making breathing difficult.
Researchers think that it’s because people who smoke weed tend to inhale a lot more.
They also hold the smoke in their lungs for up to 4 times longer than cigarette smoke.
The most surprising part of weed users’ lung conditions is the age at which they get them.
While tobacco smokers developed lung problems at an average age of 65, marijuana users developed
lung problems at an average age of 41 Alex is running out of time.
By the eighth year, Alex is tired of coughing all the time and coming down with colds and
bronchitis. So he decides to get his weed fix in other ways. That means more edibles than joints.
Maybe that will help his lungs recover. And they might - especially the more
he reduces his use - but this form of weed use carries its own risks.
Scientists recently found that any form of weed use led to potential health problems
that have nothing to do with the brain and lungs. New research discovered that
frequent weed users are at significantly increased risk of heart attacks and strokes.
The risk to Alex is no longer just cognitive. It’s a physical threat in his chest.
Daily users had 25% higher odds of having a heart attack. Even worse,
they increased their chance of stroke by 42%. To make sure the results were accurate,
researchers controlled for tobacco use among participants, since many people smoke both weed
and cigarettes. But the evidence was still there. For men under 55 and women under 65,
weed use resulted in a 36% combined increase for coronary heart disease, heart attack or stroke.
And as the study put it, “the odds were higher even when researchers looked only at those who
had never used tobacco products or e-cigarettes”. Switching from smoking to eating may take care
of Alex’s lungs. But it’s still killing his cardiovascular system.
After a couple more years of marijuana use, Alex has had enough. His work has suffered,
he feels disconnected from a lot of his friends and he wants to make a change.
He finally hears about the heart attack study and makes a decision: it’s time for him to quit.
But that’s when the scariest question of all pops up. Is the damage weed has done to his mind and
body…reversible? Or is his baseline permanently altered after his brain and heart have spent ten
years in chemical stasis? The answer is…it depends.
One study found that heavy marijuana users, and even those who had just quit, did worse in IQ,
processing speed, immediate, and delayed memory. But after 3 months of quitting weed,
they were back to their “pre-drug performance” when it came to their cognitive abilities.
But that comes with a caveat. Because another study that looked
at over 1,000 subjects found that whether you rebounded or not had a lot to do with one factor.
The age at which they started smoking. Here, Alex has something good going for him.
He hadn’t even tried weed until his last year of college. And he didn’t
become a daily user until he was almost 23. If he had started as a teenager, that might be a
different story. The large-scale study found that “cessation of cannabis use did not fully restore
neuropsychological [brain] functioning” among people who started in their teens.
The teenage brain is still morphing and developing. Reducing grey matter
and otherwise messing with CB1 receptors in a brain that’s constantly changing
causes much more damage than to an adult. But in adults, CB1 receptors can return to
normal levels even just four weeks after weed use stops. In daily users, that’s about how
long THC metabolites remain in the system. So Alex is in the clear when it comes to his
brain. Even though because of the duration and frequency of his use, it will probably
take him a lot more time to get back to his baseline than for a more “social” user.
He will also suffer through a period of insomnia and sleep difficulty. Because he was relying on
weed to sleep for so long, he will also experience weirdly, particularly vivid dreams. Experts think
that’s because Alex’s full REM cycle will come back with a bang, leading to intense dreaming.
What about Alex’s lungs? And perhaps most importantly, his heart?
Well, doctors who treat those who quit smoking weed and/or tobacco say
that “the airway inflammation and bronchitis induced by cannabis are largely reversible”.
When doctors followed up with those who quit, they were no more likely to have symptoms
like coughing, sputum, or other respiratory symptoms than those who never smoked at all.
That’s great news for Alex. He’s back at the gym, and slowly finding it easier to do his old
exercises than at any point in the past 10 years. But his lung function underneath all that hasn’t
rebounded as much as he’d hoped. One source found that after quitting weed,
“objective lung function changes are more modest than with tobacco cessation”.
One could argue that’s because tobacco damages the lungs a lot more to begin with;
but there’s just not enough research to know for sure.
Which touches on the most important part of Alex’s health after quitting: his heart condition.
Unfortunately, this is one area where we just don’t know the answer. As with most substances,
quitting leads to some improvement in his cardiovascular health.
But since marijuana was illegal for so long, many long-term effects haven’t been studied.
Overall though, things are looking up for Alex. His motivation is back,
he feels more emotionally regulated, he can run a few miles without any issues…and it seems like
his body and mind are going to be alright. Alex is going to face a few difficult months
while he detoxes… but one part might be a literal nightmare. Watch ‘What Happens to
Your Dreams When You Smoke Weed’ to see what goes on at night. Or click on this.
